solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Perhaps watch video that may rain on your parade (6,4)

definitions.text: that may rain on your parade

blocks.note: ticker is old slang for a watch; 'perhaps' flags the example

annotation.surface: Someone's viewing habits threaten to spoil a celebration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rain on your parade' means spoil your fun, but here it is literal: ticker tape is thrown down over a street parade.
annotation.definitionFit: Ticker tape is showered from windows over celebratory parades.

entries.clue: Articles about Bart’s last letter to Homer (5)

indicators.note: the articles go around the T
take only the final letter of Bart's

blocks.note: the two articles THE and A

annotation.surface: A cartoon son writes a note to his father Homer Simpson.
annotation.walkthrough: The Simpsons surface hides the other Homer: the Greek poet, whose alphabet includes theta.
annotation.definitionFit: Theta is a letter of the Greek alphabet, the one Homer wrote in.

entries.clue: Personal insult loved by a miserly director? (5,4)

blocks.note: an unfair jibe aimed at the person rather than the argument
read literally: a shot that costs little to film, which a stingy director would love

annotation.surface: A tight-fisted film director has a favourite put-down.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is whimsical: read literally, a cheap shot is an inexpensive piece of filming, which a miser behind the camera would adore.
annotation.definitionFit: A cheap shot is an unfair or spiteful personal remark.

entries.clue: Spare gold coin one splits with European is remarkable (14)

indicators.note: to split something is to break it apart, so I goes into the middle of DINAR
'with' means alongside, so E is simply attached after the rest

blocks.note: the dinar is a currency of several countries
I is the Roman one, placed inside DINAR

annotation.surface: A spare gold coin shared with a European turns out to be something special.
annotation.walkthrough: EXTRAORDINAIRE is used after a noun, as in 'a chef extraordinaire'; DINAR gets split as DINA-I-R.
annotation.definitionFit: Extraordinaire, placed after a noun, means outstanding or remarkable.

entries.clue: Arrives and spoils Pixar movie (5,2)

annotation.surface: Someone shows up and gives away the ending of a Pixar film.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' pretends to mean revealing a plot; it is milk going off.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who turns up somewhere has come or appeared there, often unexpectedly.

entries.clue: Old kingdom’s power over large country (7)

indicators.note: in a down answer, P sits above the rest

blocks.note: Russia is the largest country by area

annotation.surface: A historic kingdom once held sway over a vast neighbour.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Prussia was a German state ruled by Hohenzollern kings from 1701, abolished after the Second World War.

entries.clue: Tunisia’s capital missing from book of maps, regrettably (4)

definitions.note: ALAS is an interjection; 'regrettably' is an adverb, but both work as sentence openers.

indicators.note: the capital letter of Tunisia is its first, T
something missing from a place is absent, so T must be taken away from the atlas

blocks.note: an atlas is a book of maps

annotation.surface: Sadly, Tunis has been left out of the atlas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital' tempts you to think of Tunis; it only means the first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Alas is an exclamation of regret, so it can stand for 'regrettably'.

entries.clue: Grub is something very hot, reportedly (5)

indicators.note: a report is something heard

blocks.note: lava, molten rock; British speech drops the R, so the two words sound the same

annotation.surface: Someone warns that the food is scorching.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like food, but it is an insect grub; the homophone relies on British speech, where the R in LARVA is silent.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a grub is the soft wormlike young stage of a beetle or similar insect.

entries.clue: What “decreases” rations — me unfortunately (5,4)

indicators.note: the letters have come out badly, i.e. jumbled

annotation.surface: Someone complains that it is their rations being cut.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks tell you to read 'decreases' as de-creases: removes creases, which is what a steam iron does.
annotation.definitionFit: A steam iron takes the creases out of clothes.

entries.clue: Fresh food and shower before nap? Tuck in here! (8,6)

indicators.note: the letters of FOOD and SHOWER are made anew
the anagram comes ahead of REST

annotation.surface: Snack, shower, then a snooze: time to tuck in to a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tuck in' reads as an invitation to eat, but Tuck is Friar Tuck, Robin Hood's companion, who lived in Sherwood Forest.
annotation.definitionFit: Friar Tuck, of the Robin Hood legend, is found in Sherwood Forest.

entries.clue: Regularly leave key equestrian competitor (7)

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so take letters spaced evenly through leave

blocks.note: the Enter key on a keyboard

annotation.surface: Someone habitually leaves the key behind.
annotation.walkthrough: An eventer is a horse or rider in eventing: dressage, cross-country and show jumping.
annotation.definitionFit: An eventer competes in equestrian three-day events.

entries.clue: Break shoe, run and throw? (7)

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and rearranged

annotation.surface: A runner snaps a shoe mid-stride and flings it away.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks 'throw' as an example: a horse throws its rider, which unhorses them. Shoe fits the horse theme too.
annotation.definitionFit: Throw here is what a bucking horse does to its rider; unseating them from the saddle is the sense.

entries.clue: Evaluates software associated with lifts (9)

blocks.note: an app is a piece of software

annotation.surface: Someone reviews the software that runs a building's elevators.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lifts' pretends to be the British noun for elevators; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean judging the worth or quality of something, like a valuer pricing property.

entries.clue: Empire in complete mess at the outset (5)

indicators.note: take only the first letter of mess

blocks.note: as in 'a real mess' = a complete mess

annotation.surface: An empire was in a total shambles from the very beginning.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase 'complete mess' has to be split: complete gives REAL, and mess gives only its M.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name a territory ruled by a sovereign, whether kingdom or empire.

entries.clue: Detest drab horticulture displays (5)

indicators.note: the phrase shows the answer within it

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between drab and horticulture

annotation.surface: Someone hates dreary garden displays.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Displays' reads as a noun, flower displays; it is the verb that shows the hidden word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to loathe something intensely, regarding it with disgust.

entries.clue: Columnist from Guyana not wrong (5,4)

indicators.note: the letters are put wrongly, i.e. rearranged

annotation.surface: A writer from Guyana is proved right.
annotation.walkthrough: An agony aunt is the British term for a newspaper advice columnist.
annotation.definitionFit: An agony aunt writes an advice column answering readers' problems.

entries.clue: Games a police chief overheard in thick fog (3-6)

indicators.note: what is heard, not what is written

blocks.note: super = superintendent, a senior police officer
said aloud, PE + A + SUPER gives the sound of the foggy term

annotation.surface: A police chief overhears some games while lost in dense fog.
annotation.walkthrough: A pea-souper is an old London smog as thick and yellow as pea soup.
annotation.definitionFit: The London smogs of the past were thick and yellow-green like pea soup, hence the nickname.

entries.clue: Wage produced from plain writing? Sweet! (9)

annotation.surface: Someone is delighted to earn a salary from straightforward writing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wage' is not pay but the verb, as in to wage or prosecute a war.
annotation.definitionFit: Wage is the verb here: one wages or pursues a war or campaign, carrying it through to conclusion.

entries.clue: Tell me, using your brain, best sock (3,4,2)

blocks.note: to outwit is to best someone by cleverness

annotation.surface: Someone asks to be told how to choose the best sock by thinking about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sock' is not clothing but a blow; OUTWIT and HIT overlap nothing, they simply join.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Out with it!' is a demand to tell me what you're keeping back.

entries.clue: Cool to live without working body part (7)

indicators.note: outside: BE goes round ON

blocks.note: to be is to live, exist
on = working, as a switched-on machine

annotation.surface: Someone thinks it would be cool to live without work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the old sense of outside, as in the hymn's 'a green hill far away, without a city wall', not lacking.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: this bone forming the pelvis is one particular part of the skeleton.

entries.clue: Couple raised farm animal during work (7)

indicators.note: in a down answer, lifting SOW turns it upside down
something happening during an event occurs inside its span, so WOS goes inside TOME

blocks.note: a tome is a (large) written work
a sow is a female pig

annotation.surface: A pair brought up a farm animal while at work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Raised' reads as reared, as farmers raise animals; in a down clue it means written upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name a pair of people, especially partners in a relationship or game.

entries.clue: Be overwhelmed with new information from the east (5)

indicators.note: read right to left, from east to west

annotation.surface: Someone is swamped by fresh news arriving from the East.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface fits 'drowning in information'; 'from the east' is an across-clue reversal instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: we speak of drowning in paperwork or emails when there is simply too much to cope with.

entries.clue: US college briefly thanks conference venue (5)

indicators.note: cut short: YALE loses its last letter

blocks.note: ta is British slang for thanks

annotation.surface: A student thanks an American university for hosting a conference.
annotation.walkthrough: Yalta, in Crimea, hosted the 1945 conference of Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: this Crimean resort hosted Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin in February 1945.

entries.clue: Enter gate-keeper’s residence (5)

blocks.note: formal sense: to register a complaint or appeal officially
the small house at the entrance to a country estate

annotation.surface: An invitation to step into the gatekeeper's house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Enter' is the formal sense, as in lodging or entering a complaint.
annotation.definitionFit: A lodge is the small house by an estate's gate, where the gatekeeper lives.

entries.clue: Champion rugby player playing in French team initially (9)

indicators.note: take only the first letter of team

blocks.note: a prop is a forward in the rugby scrum
on = playing, as an actor on stage

annotation.surface: A top rugby player turns out for a French side.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Champion' looks like a winner, but it is one who champions a cause.
annotation.definitionFit: A proponent champions, or argues for, a cause.

entries.clue: Be anxious when losing opener for lock (5)

indicators.note: the opener is the first letter, the one that opens the word, and losing it removes it

blocks.note: to stress is to be anxious
the S at the front is removed

annotation.surface: Someone worries about losing the key to a lock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opener' and 'lock' pair up as key and lock; the lock is a lock of hair.
annotation.definitionFit: A lock is a curl or strand of hair, and so is a tress, a slightly poetic word.

entries.clue: Doctor urged on to get experience (7)

indicators.note: to doctor is to alter or tamper with

annotation.surface: A doctor is pushed to gain experience.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a person, but it is the verb meaning tamper with.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to go through or suffer something, such as surgery or training.

entries.clue: Rely excessively on old and extremely vulnerable scheme (7)

indicators.note: take the letters at the extremes

blocks.note: first and last letters of vulnerable
a ruse is a scheme or trick

annotation.surface: Someone depends too much on an old, very shaky plan.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' pretends to mean very; it asks for the two ends of vulnerable.
annotation.definitionFit: To overuse something is to rely on it too much.

entries.clue: Level of drop in sound (4)

indicators.note: what the word sounds like

blocks.note: a tear, the drop from an eye; the two words sound identical

annotation.surface: A question of how far the volume has dropped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drop in sound' reads like a fall in volume; drop is a teardrop.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tier is one row or rank stacked above another, like seating in a stadium.

entries.clue: Persistent about fast time? Not so much (10)

blocks.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting

annotation.surface: Someone who keeps going on about fasting is told to cut down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fast time' suggests speed; it is a period of fasting.
annotation.definitionFit: Relentless means persistent, never letting up.
